headline: High-risk shared write surfaces and autonomous action scopes create dangerous default conflict and leakage pathways between Devin and ECC.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Devin can read/write cloud workspace files and use MCP; ECC also writes files and uses MCP, so a shared file or MCP bridge could carry attacker-controlled instructions. Neither profile proves a direct default ingestion path, so this is not high. The interaction risk is plausible from both agents’ documented surfaces.
conditions: IF Devin and ECC are connected through a shared filesystem or MCP server
IF either agent parses the other’s file output as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers between the two agents
Separate their workspace roots and repo clones
Add provenance tags to any handoff files
Require manual review before one agent consumes the other’s output
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitizing wrappers on shared channels

B_data_leakage.rationale: Devin handles repo deploy keys and integration tokens, while ECC touches session summaries, hooks, and agent definitions in local config paths. Devin’s broad network egress and Slack/Jira/Notion writes plus ECC’s file surfaces create a realistic path for sensitive workspace data to leak across a shared environment. The profiles do not show isolation strong enough to reduce this below high.
conditions: IF both agents run on the same machine or shared workspace
IF sensitive repo or session data is present in files accessible to both agents
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate OS user or container
Keep secrets out of shared workspace files
Rotate any tokens exposed to either agent
Restrict outbound network destinations for the agent handling secrets
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. Devin’s shared state via integrations and ECC’s session-file boundary make concurrent writes to the same repo or config paths likely to collide without locking. That overlap matches the rubric’s dangerous default write-conflict pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or shared config directory
IF no external lock or merge coordinator serializes their writes
mitigations: Assign separate branches or worktrees
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Split config directories per agent
Pause one agent while the other commits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Devin is an autonomous planner-executor, and ECC’s skills/subagents surface encourages delegated workflows; either can treat the other’s output as authoritative. If Devin generates facts or code changes that ECC then acts on, errors can cascade into commits or downstream actions. The profiles show no built-in verification step between them.
conditions: IF one agent’s output is fed directly into the other’s workflow
IF the receiving agent does not independently verify claims before acting
mitigations: Require human approval before downstream actions
Insert a verification step between agents
Limit one agent to drafting only
Use checklists for code or config changes
requires-engineering: add structured provenance and validation gates

E_compliance.rationale: Devin explicitly handles Slack, Jira, and Notion data plus repo secrets, while ECC touches session summaries, hooks, and security findings in local config paths. If regulated or sensitive data is routed through both, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not specify a direct residency mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated personal or customer data is stored in either agent’s workspace
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two systems
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces
Document retention settings for both agents
Delete stale session artifacts regularly
Restrict sensitive data to one compliant system
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
